ai-at-work.title: Why the rise of open source AI isn’t hurting Anthropic … yet
ai-at-work.excerpt: Open source models’ success isn’t coming at the expense of frontier labs. Instead, they each seem to capture two phases of the same life cycle.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Open source AI models are thriving without cannibalizing commercial players like Anthropic because they're serving different market phases. For digital workplace pros, this matters because it means your AI tooling landscape stays fragmented across open and proprietary options, forcing you to evaluate cost versus control versus capability for each use case. Honestly, it's the same pattern we saw with Linux and enterprise software thirty years ago, except now it moves at internet speed and costs actual jobs to figure out which stack to bet on.

ai-at-work.title: Microsoft joins AI cost-cutting trend by relying more on its own models
ai-at-work.excerpt: Microsoft is the latest Silicon Valley giant to cut back on its AI spending.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Microsoft is shifting away from relying heavily on external AI models and building more of its own in-house, part of a broader cost-cutting trend across Big Tech. This matters to digital workplace pros because it signals that the AI gold rush is cooling down and companies are getting serious about actual ROI instead of just throwing money at every shiny model that hits the market. After years of watching enterprise leaders chase every new AI tool like it was the last lifeboat, this is refreshingly honest: turns out you can't solve every workplace problem by bolting on another AI service.

ai-at-work.dwp_take: Meta released Muse Image, an AI model that generates images while also handling coding tasks and web searches. For digital workplace pros, this matters because image generation is increasingly embedded in productivity tools, so understanding these capabilities helps you evaluate what's actually useful versus what's marketing noise. Honestly, if Meta is bundling coding and search into an image generator, someone's trying to solve five problems at once when most teams just need one thing that actually works reliably.

ai-at-work.title: Microsoft is reportedly ditching OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s AI models in favor of its own to cut costs
ai-at-work.excerpt: Microsoft Corp. is reportedly transitioning away from using OpenAI Group PBC’s and Anthropic PBC’s most advanced artificial intelligence models in favor of its own — increasingly leaning on the new Mi
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Microsoft is moving its internal AI workloads away from OpenAI and Anthropic models to use its own MAI models instead, primarily to reduce costs. This matters to digital workplace pros because if Microsoft is betting its own infrastructure on MAI, those models will inevitably flow into workplace tools like Copilot and Teams faster than a Monday morning all-hands meeting. The irony is delicious: Microsoft publicly says its own AI isn't as good, then quietly bets the farm on it anyway because the spreadsheet said to.

tools-tech.title: Anthropic shines a light into the Claude AI black hole
tools-tech.excerpt: Anthropic has found a way to shed new light on how its models solve problems, thanks to its discovery of what it has dubbed the J-space. “We find that Claude has developed a small collection of intern
tools-tech.dwp_take: Anthropic has discovered something called J-space, a set of internal neural patterns that appear to play an outsized role in how Claude AI models solve problems, making their decision-making process somewhat more transparent. For digital workplace pros deploying AI tools, understanding what's actually happening inside these black boxes matters because you need to know if you can trust the outputs your organization is depending on. Here's the thing though: we've been promised "explainable AI" before, and I'll believe it when I can walk a board member through exactly why Claude rejected that expense report without needing a PhD in mathematics.

digital-culture.dwp_take: Microsoft cut 4,800 jobs yesterday, with 3,200 coming from Xbox, including a VP who'd been there 37 years. This matters because it shows even specialized tech talent with deep institutional knowledge gets caught in reorganizations, which should make any digital workplace leader think twice about how they retain expertise. Turns out being loyal to one company for nearly four decades doesn't buy you much job security anymore, which is pretty bleak when you think about it.
